title: A Single Blood Test Can Now Screen for 10 Cancers — and Zydus and Apollo Are Bringing It to India
excerpt: The FDA-designated multi-cancer detection test, built by Guardant Health, uses a simple blood draw to catch bladder, breast, colorectal and seven other cancers before symptoms appear
body:
A single blood draw could soon screen for ten of the most common cancers in India — and two of the country's biggest healthcare names are joining forces to make it happen.

Zydus Lifesciences and Apollo Hospitals announced on Friday that they have signed a memorandum of understanding to bring Guardant Health's multi-cancer detection (MCD) blood test to India. The test, which has received Breakthrough Device Designation from the US Food and Drug Administration, uses methylation-based technology to detect cancer signals from a single blood sample — no invasive biopsy, no imaging appointment, no hospital stay.

The screening covers ten cancers: bladder, breast, colorectal, oesophageal, gastric, liver, lung, ovarian, pancreatic and prostate. It is designed for individuals aged 45 and above who are at average risk — a demographic that includes millions of Indians and members of the diaspora who currently have limited access to systematic multi-cancer screening.

## Why This Matters for India

India diagnoses roughly 1.4 million new cancer cases annually, and more than two-thirds are detected at advanced stages when treatment options are limited and costs spiral. For cancers such as pancreatic, ovarian and liver — which have no widely recommended single-organ screening test — late detection is often a death sentence. A single blood test that can flag signals across multiple cancer types could fundamentally shift the diagnosis timeline.

"At Apollo, we have long believed that the most effective healthcare is proactive healthcare," said Dr Prathap C. Reddy, chairman of Apollo Hospitals Group. "The future of medicine lies not only in treating disease, but in preventing it and detecting it at its earliest, most treatable stages."

Dr Sharvil Patel, managing director of Zydus Lifesciences, described the partnership as an effort to "reimagine cancer diagnostics in India and expand access to newer screening technologies."

Under the arrangement, Zydus holds the exclusive rights to market Guardant Health's test in India, while Apollo Hospitals will serve as the clinical partner offering the screening service through its nationwide hospital network — the largest private healthcare system in the country, with more than 70 hospitals across India.

## The Technology Behind It

The test works by analysing cell-free DNA circulating in the blood for methylation patterns that are characteristic of cancer. Unlike genetic tests that look for inherited mutations, methylation-based assays detect epigenetic changes — chemical modifications to DNA that tumour cells shed into the bloodstream. This approach can identify cancer signals even before symptoms appear.

Guardant Health's Shield test, as the MCD platform is known commercially, completed a pivotal clinical trial of more than 10,000 participants. Its earlier colorectal-specific version received FDA approval in 2024, and the broader multi-cancer version received Breakthrough Device Designation — a category the FDA reserves for technologies that offer a meaningful advance over existing options.

## The Diaspora Angle

For the estimated 32 million Indians living abroad, the partnership carries particular relevance. Cancer screening protocols in the US, UK and Canada remain largely organ-specific — a colonoscopy here, a mammogram there — with no single test covering multiple cancers simultaneously. Many NRIs already schedule health check-ups during visits to India, drawn by lower costs and shorter wait times. A validated multi-cancer blood test available through Apollo's network could become a powerful draw for preventive health tourism.

South Asians also face distinctive cancer risks. Studies have documented elevated rates of oral, oesophageal and gallbladder cancers linked to dietary habits, tobacco use patterns and genetic predisposition. Breast and cervical cancers are diagnosed at younger ages in South Asian women compared with Western populations. A screening test tailored for the 45-plus age group addresses the demographic window where these risks intensify.

## What Comes Next

The partnership is still in its early stages — no pricing has been announced, and regulatory approvals specific to India's Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation may be required before widespread deployment. But the combination of Zydus's diagnostic distribution infrastructure, Apollo's clinical reach and Guardant's proven technology creates a platform that could scale rapidly once cleared.

India's cancer diagnostics market is projected to reach $3.2 billion by 2028, driven by rising awareness and government initiatives such as the National Programme for Prevention and Control of Cancer. The Zydus-Apollo-Guardant partnership is a bet that the future of cancer screening lies in simplicity — a single tube of blood, tested once, covering the cancers that kill the most people.
